claims.sentence: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection.
claims.evidence: NHS: sepsis is a serious reaction to infection that can be life-threatening.

claims.sentence: The NHS describes it as a medical emergency.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says it develops quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital; the phrase 'medical emergency' was not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says it can develop very quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital.

claims.sentence: It can happen after a bacterial infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.
claims.evidence: NHS lists chest infections (pneumonia), UTIs and skin infections such as cellulitis as common triggers; 'bacterial' was not stated.
claims.newSentence: It can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.

claims.sentence: The exact cause is not always clear.
claims.evidence: NHS: the exact cause is not known; the immune system is thought to overreact to an infection.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, and blue, pale, grey or blotchy skin.
claims.evidence: Retrieved list: confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, trouble breathing, blue, pale or blotchy skin. 'Grey' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, and blue, pale or blotchy skin.

claims.sentence: Not passing urine for a long period is another sign.
claims.evidence: NHS adult wording retrieved: not peeing all day or peeing very little in the past 18 hours. 'Long period' is vaguer than the page.
claims.newSentence: Passing no urine all day, or very little, is another sign.

claims.sentence: A high temperature is less common in older adults, so a person can have sepsis without a fever.
claims.evidence: Search for this explicitly found no NHS text saying a high temperature is less common in older adults. NHS lists a very high OR low temperature.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists fast or difficult breathing, a fit (seizure), mottled, bluish or pale skin, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it, and being unusually sleepy or hard to wake.
claims.evidence: Retrieved for babies/children: fast or hard breathing, rash that does not fade under a glass (rare in sepsis, may be meningitis), unusual sleepiness, poor feeding; blue/pale/blotchy skin in general list. Fit, mottled and 'hard to wake' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: For babies and young children, the NHS lists fast or difficult breathing, blue, pale or blotchy skin, being unusually sleepy, and a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.

claims.sentence: In young children, refusing feeds or repeated vomiting can also be signs.
claims.evidence: Poor feeding retrieved; repeated vomiting not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: In babies and young children, poor feeding can also be a sign.

claims.sentence: Sepsis mostly affects very young children, older adults and people with underlying health conditions.
claims.evidence: NHS: anyone can get sepsis, but the chance is higher for babies under 12 months and people over 75; 'mostly' not supported.
claims.newSentence: Anyone can get sepsis, but the chance is higher in babies under 12 months and people over 75.

claims.sentence: It can sometimes occur in people who are otherwise fit and healthy.
claims.evidence: NHS: anyone can get sepsis.

claims.sentence: People with weakened immune systems, including those on long-term steroids or other medicines that suppress the immune system, are also at higher risk.
claims.evidence: NHS lists weakened immune system from conditions such as HIV or sickle cell disease, chemotherapy, or taking corticosteroids or immunosuppressants. 'Long-term' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: People with a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy or from taking corticosteroids or other medicines that suppress the immune system, are also at higher risk.

claims.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or child shows signs of sepsis, or if there is a worry that it could be sepsis.
claims.evidence: NHS: if you think you or your child may have sepsis, call 999 or go to A&E; if unsure it is still better to call 999.

claims.sentence: It advises asking someone to drive, or calling for an ambulance, rather than driving oneself.
claims.evidence: NHS Wales page: ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance; do not drive yourself to A&E. NHS England page summary also says don't drive yourself.

claims.sentence: Some local NHS guidance gives a middle route for less certain cases: an urgent GP or urgent treatment centre visit, or NHS 111.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: if worried about an infection but sepsis is not suspected, call NHS 111 or contact your GP; NHS 111 also advised if sepsis in past 12 months with infection symptoms. Urgent treatment centre not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: If you are worried about an infection but do not think it is sepsis, you can call NHS 111 or contact your GP.

claims.sentence: If the person seems seriously unwell, the safe route is 999.
claims.evidence: Implies 999 only if seriously unwell, which could reassure wrongly; NHS says call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis may be present, and if unsure it is still better to call 999.
claims.newSentence: If you are unsure whether it could be sepsis, the NHS says it is still better to call 999.

claims.sentence: Sepsis is treated in hospital.
claims.evidence: NHS: treatment happens in hospital.

claims.sentence: Treatment includes antibiotics, oxygen to help with breathing, and fluids given into a vein.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: antibiotics, oxygen if needed, intravenous fluids.
claims.newSentence: Treatment usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids given into a vein.

claims.sentence: Some people need intensive care.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: some patients need intensive care.

claims.sentence: Recovery can take weeks or months.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says post-sepsis syndrome often lasts 6 to 18 months and some take longer; 'weeks or months' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Recovery can take a long time, and some people take months or longer to feel back to normal.

claims.sentence: Some people have longer-lasting problems after sepsis, such as tiredness and changes in mood, which is sometimes called post-sepsis syndrome.
claims.evidence: Post-sepsis syndrome can cause tiredness, low mood, memory or concentration problems.

claims.sentence: Sepsis is a medical emergency that can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.
claims.evidence: 'Medical emergency' wording not retrieved; see c02.
claims.newSentence: Sepsis can be life-threatening and needs urgent hospital treatment; it can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.

claims.sentence: Signs in adults include confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing and blue, pale or blotchy skin.
claims.evidence: Matches retrieved adult list.

claims.sentence: Signs in babies and children include fast or difficult breathing, a fit, mottled or pale skin, and a rash that does not fade under pressure.
claims.evidence: Fit and mottled not retrieved; see c08.
claims.newSentence: Signs in babies and children include fast or difficult breathing, unusual sleepiness, poor feeding, and a rash that does not fade under a glass.

claims.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if someone may have sepsis, and not to drive there.
claims.evidence: See c13 and c14.

claims.sentence: Treatment is in hospital and includes antibiotics, oxygen and fluids into a vein.
claims.evidence: Oxygen only 'if needed'; see c18.
claims.newSentence: Treatment is in hospital and usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids into a vein.

claims.sentence: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection; the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis is suspected.
claims.evidence: See c01 and c13.

notes: Search summaries blend pages. Non-fading rash is, per NHS, rare in sepsis but may signal meningitis; consider saying so. Urine thresholds differ by age/trust (under 5s: none in 12 hours); no hour figures were added to the guide. 'Do not drive' attributed to NHS Wales page (111.wales.nhs.uk/Sepsis/) as well as the NHS England page. High-temperature-in-older-adults claim could not be verified and was removed. Search 4 results were NHS trust and Wales pages, not national NHS England guidance, for the 111/GP route.
